figures.caption: Fig. 1. Design, sensing and control of the robotic analog. (A) Conceptual schematic comparing the biological motor system and the robotic analog. The biological system integrates multiple feedback signals (e.g., vision, joint angle, muscle length) to control muscle actuation via the brain; the robotic analog replicates this structure through artificial muscles, proprioceptive sensing, and visual feedback, enabling closed-loop control via an ANN controller. (B) Self-sensing mechanism of biological muscle and artificial muscle. (C) Overview of the end-to-end reinforcement learning framework. The actor network receives multi-modal input and directly outputs stimulating currents to the artificial muscles. (D) Reaching error of ANN controllers
Fig. 2. Functional similarity between the robotic analog and the biological motor system. (A) The robot arm maintained accurate trajectories despite various unexpected artificial muscle damages. (B)

Fig. 3. Physical effect of rotational neural dynamics on movement. (A) Schematic illustration of the extraction process of the “jPC1-reconstructed” movement, representing movement dominated by rotational dynamics. (B) The distribution of the “jPC1-reconstructed” movement relative to the direction of the singlepoint reaching task (reaching direction), by the “Vis” model. The right panel shows the physical implication of the rotational dynamics. (C) The distribution of the angle (𝜃) between “jPC1-reconstructed” movement and the reaching direction under different feedback combinations. (D) The distribution of 𝑠𝑖𝑛(𝜃) and velocity during single point reaching tasks under different feedback combinations. (E) The distribution of the angle 𝜃 between “jPC1-reconstructed” movement and the reaching direction with different control channels. (F) The distribution of 𝑠𝑖𝑛(𝜃) and velocity during single point reaching task with different control channels. (G) The actual reaching trajectories of the monkey, compared with the CCA projections of the neural population response and the reconstructed jPC1 signal. Fig. 4. Effect of sensory feedback and motor redundancy on neural and muscle energy. (A) Schematic of the actor networks with different sensory inputs. Each network consists of an input linear layer, an RNN layer (LSTM), and an output linear layer to control motor current. (B and C) Neural activities of the “Vis” model and the “Len+Ang+Vis” model driving the robot arm to reach the same point (𝑥,𝑦,𝑧)=(3, 0, 1). The subplots below B and C show the corresponding total neural energy, calculated as the squared sum of all neural activities. (D) Average neural energy over time of the RNN layer in actor network under different feedback combinations. (E) Muscle activation pattern of the robot arm at 5 second during reaching with 12 control channels by the “Vis” model. (F and G) Muscle lengths over time of the robot arm by the “Vis” model and the “Len+Ang+Vis” model, respectively. (H) Total muscle energy, calculated as the work done by the electric currents, of the robot arm under different feedback combinations. (I–K) Corresponding stimulating currents for the artificial muscles during reaching with I-12, J-6,and K-3 control channels. (L) Neural and muscle energy of the robot arm with different control channels.

Fig. 5. Changes of neural population dynamics and motor performance during the learning process. (A) Training protocol of the robot arm, which is driven to achieve optimal accuracy, as well as collecting most bonuses in a given time window. (B) The experimental setup of the robot arm. Six motion capture cameras are mounted on a custom metal frame to track the spatial coordinates of the marker on the end effector. Muscle length data is collected by the control circuit. Joint angle data is directly received by the computer via the serial port. The actor network generates control signals that are converted to 12 electric current outputs for the artificial muscles.
